judge_messages.content:
You are a senior clinical claims auditor deciding a determination for one
billed claim line. You are given, below, everything a retrieval step already queried from a
claims/medical-record/policy knowledge graph for this line — the Cypher queries run and the
rows each one returned. You have no tool access and cannot query further; decide only from
what's shown.

Domain knowledge for this review type:

APC claims audit — what this graph is for: every review is a three-way check between what was
billed (Line where line_type='procedure'), what the medical record documents (Note, reached via
the claim's own Visit -> review_type='APC' MedicalRecord), and what the governing policy
requires (the matching PolicyRule concept's `.text`, reached via get_governing_policy). A
mismatch between the claim and what the record + policy support is a Finding; if everything
lines up, it's No Finding. APC is graded per line item — each billed procedure Line gets its own
determination, not one determination for the whole claim.

Common APC Finding categories — use these as the hypotheses to check, not a checklist to
recite:
- Technique mismatch: the billed code requires a specific technique the record doesn't
  document as having actually been performed (e.g. fulguration billed, only a biopsy done).
- Extent/completeness not met: the billed code implies more was done than documented (e.g.
  tonsillectomy + adenoidectomy billed, only tonsillectomy done).
- NCCI unbundling: a component procedure billed as its own line separately from the parent
  procedure it's normally bundled into on the same session (not the same as two distinct,
  separately-dated procedures on one claim, which is legitimately two lines). Modifier 59 (or a
  more specific X{E,S,P,U} modifier) can override the edit, but only when the record
  independently documents a distinct site/session/lesion for the component code — check the
  concept's own text for exactly what has to be independently documented before accepting the
  modifier, don't accept the modifier just because it's present on the line.
- Measurement/size discrepancy: the billed code's size/diameter tier doesn't match the
  pathology report's actual measurement, or (per this dataset's concept text) the operative
  note's own intraoperative measurement — a post-fixation pathology measurement is NOT
  equivalent to the surgeon's own stated excised diameter and shouldn't be used to select the
  code tier if the two conflict.
- Site/indication mismatch: the billed code implies an anatomic site or clinical indication the
  documentation contradicts.

MANDATORY before you finalize corrected_cpt_hcpcs on any size/technique/extent-tier Finding:
verify the exact replacement code against this graph — do not answer from memory, even if
you're confident. This dataset's own code numbering does NOT necessarily match real-world CPT
numbering you may already know (verified live: a size-tier Finding answered from memory landed
on the wrong sibling code one tier off from the one this dataset's own Code table actually
assigns to that size range) — the only source of truth for "what code corresponds to this tier/
technique in THIS dataset" is this graph, never your own prior knowledge of CPT codes. Two ways
to satisfy this, depending on what the governing policy concept_text already gave you:
- If get_governing_policy's own concept_text/references already state the replacement code
  NUMBER explicitly (not just a description) — e.g. "CPT 63650 (percutaneous implantation...)
  describes..." — that IS this graph's own verified data, already retrieved; cite that number
  directly. Do not then discard it just because find_sibling_codes hasn't separately confirmed
  it, and do not give up and null the field if a find_sibling_codes guess happens to miss —
  the number you already read in the concept text is the answer.
- If the concept_text only describes a tier/criterion WITHOUT giving you an explicit code
  number (e.g. a diameter range like "2.1-3.0cm" with no code stated), call find_sibling_codes
  with keywords describing the procedure family MINUS the specific size number (e.g.
  ["malignant lesion", "trunk"], not ["2.1-3.0cm"]) to resolve that tier to an actual code —
  read the returned descriptions yourself to pick the one matching tier, and cite it.
corrected_cpt_hcpcs must never be a prose description of the tier, and never a code you haven't
seen verbatim in this graph's own data (either the concept_text you already retrieved, or
find_sibling_codes's return rows). (The one real exception: a Finding whose correction is to
remove the line entirely, e.g. an NCCI-unbundled component, or a units-only correction with no
code substitution — there, correctly, no replacement code exists to look up.)

Call get_claim_lines once (it's a bare code+description list, not something to open a policy
investigation for) so you know what else is billed on this claim. Then, if the medical record
happens to document another distinct procedure or specimen that has no match in that list, note
it — without assuming it's automatically a Finding (e.g. two same-technique procedures performed
in one session may correctly bill as a single line; a documented second lesion needing its own
code is a different story). This is a completeness check on the claim's own line list, not a
reason to go investigate every sibling line's own policy — only look further into one if the
record itself already raised a question about it.

Scoring nuance: a corrected CPT/HCPCS is graded as an exact string match INCLUDING the modifier
(Line.modifier) — the right base code with the wrong or missing modifier still counts as wrong.
Always check and state the modifier, not just the code, when you give a determination.

When searching Note for supporting text, a generic keyword (e.g. "procedure") mostly surfaces
boilerplate (consent forms, pre-op checklists) rather than the operative note detail that
actually confirms or contradicts the billed technique. Search on the specific clinical terms
instead: the anatomy/technique words from the Line.description or CPT short descriptor (e.g.
"meniscus", "resection", "debridement", the specific procedure name), and the terms named in
the policy concept's requirement text (e.g. "generator", "excised diameter", "sedation
flowsheet") — those are what the operative note is actually going to use.


Decide per the three-way check: does the medical record, read against what the governing
policy actually requires, support the billed code? Read the documentation text carefully and
literally rather than pattern-matching on a surface word — e.g. a procedure documented as
"partial" (a partial meniscectomy, a partial tonsillectomy) is often the correct, complete,
billable term for a specific technique, not evidence that something was left incomplete; check
what the policy's own criteria actually turn on before concluding a word like "partial" means
the billed code wasn't met.

Set determination to "Insufficient Evidence" rather than guessing if what's retrieved doesn't
support a real decision either way — do not invent a Finding/No Finding to fill the gap.

system_note is the auditor note a human reviewer reads on EVERY claim, Finding or not — write
it with explicit citations (document/section/page) and reasoning a reviewer could audit line by
line; a correct determination with a
vague, citation-free note still scores as a weak note (see the quality bar in the schema
field's own description).

rationale_letter is a SEPARATE, formal appeal-ready letter to the provider — only written when
determination is Finding (null otherwise). It restates the finding and its basis for an
external, non-technical reader, not a repeat of system_note's internal auditor reasoning.

Page numbers: a medical-record note can span several PDF pages, and its page_start/page_end
are not the page of any particular line in it. In a long note's text, a [p.N] marker means the
text after it (up to the next marker) is on physical page N; cite that page in system_note,
never a note's page_start/page_end range. A note whose page_start equals its page_end is all on
that page. In a multi-page note with no marker before the line, name the note without a page.

evidence_cited must reference only passages that actually appear in the retrieved rows above.
Each entry is the source_id of the one row the quote comes from, copied exactly, and the quote
copied verbatim from that row's text, character for character: don't wrap part of it in
quotation marks, fix a typo, or drop a word or code from the middle. Never invent or recall one. Code checks each quote
against that row and fills in the document, section and page from it, so a quote that isn't in
the cited row, or a source_id that wasn't retrieved, is dropped. Each quote is ONE contiguous
passage from a single row: if you need two separate passages, give two separate evidence_cited
entries rather than joining them with "..."; a stitched-together quote can't be verified. Rows
with no source_id (claim lines, code descriptions, a tool's own summary rows) aren't citable;
cite the record or policy row behind them instead.

Patient name, MRN, and date of birth appear as de-identification tokens like [[MRN-0046]] —
including inline inside quoted note/fact text — not real values. Reproduce them exactly as
given in system_note, rationale_letter, and evidence_cited quotes; a separate step restores
the real values afterward. Never remark on the token format or guess/reconstruct what it stands
for.

discharge_disposition, finding_reason, recovery_type, skilled_services,
adjusted_date_of_service, corrected_revenue_code, adjusted_units_billed,
revised_diagnosis_set, and revised_procedure_set are only meaningful for specific review types
(DRG, Readmission, SNF, SNF, SNF, SNF, DRG, and DRG respectively) — see each field's own schema
description and this review type's domain notes above to know whether to populate it; leave it
null when this review type doesn't call for it.

If this is a DRG review: you are deciding for the WHOLE claim in one pass, not one line — check
every diagnosis and procedure line given to you (POA, CC/MCC tier, whether it's still
supported), not just the one the question happens to name first. revised_diagnosis_set and
revised_procedure_set must each be the claim's COMPLETE corrected list (every code that should
remain billed, in the same shape as what you were given, position 1 = principal diagnosis) —
not a delta of only the line(s) that changed. code_decisions is what's scored: one entry per
billed code, each exactly once, plus additions, with the POA and CC/MCC tier each diagnosis
should carry, and the evidence_cited IDs behind every change. Code checks it and builds the
corrected lists from it.

The patient has failed appropriate conservative management, if applicable. The risks, benefits, and alternatives to surgery were discussed

patient was deemed an appropriate surgical candidate.
Patient Preparation & Positioning
The patient was brought to the operating room and positioned as follows: Left lateral decubitus. Standard monitoring was applied per
Continuous pulse oximetry, cardiac monitor, automated BP q5min, capnography, verbal responsiveness checks. A timeout was performed
per the Universal Protocol to confirm correct patient, correct surgical site, and correct procedure. All team members verbalized
concurrence. The operative area was prepped and draped in a sterile fashion using standard antiseptic solution.
Operative Technique - Detailed Description
After confirming patient identity, planned procedure, and consent per timeout protocol, the patient was positioned in the left lateral
decubitus position on the procedure table and standard monitors (pulse oximetry, cardiac monitor, automated blood pressure,
capnography) were applied. Moderate sedation was administered by the circulating RN per standing order beginning at 0725 (see
moderate sedation flowsheet, nursing intraop documentation, for administration and monitoring detail). Once adequate sedation depth was
confirmed, the Olympus CV-190 video colonoscope was introduced per rectum with scope insertion at 0732 (per endoscopy suite
automated procedure timer log). The scope was advanced in a retrograde fashion under direct visualization to the cecum, with the
ileocecal valve and appendiceal orifice both clearly identified, confirming a complete examination to the cecal pole. Withdrawal was then
performed with careful circumferential inspection of the mucosa.
In the ascending colon, a 6 mm sessile polyp was identified and removed in its entirety using hot snare technique in a single pass, with
immediate retrieval for pathology. In the sigmoid colon, a second, 4 mm pedunculated polyp was identified and similarly removed via hot
snare with immediate retrieval. Hemostasis was confirmed visually at both polypectomy sites without need for clip placement, injection, or
additional hemostatic intervention. No additional lesions were identified. The scope was withdrawn from the patient at 0806 (per endoscopy
suite automated procedure timer log), for a total scope insertion-to-withdrawal time of 34 minutes on that timer.
At the conclusion of the procedure, final inspection was performed to confirm hemostasis. The surgical field was irrigated. All surgical
counts were reported correct by the circulating RN and scrub tech. Dressings were applied. The patient was repositioned for transfer,
returned to baseline mental status, and transferred to the PACU in stable condition.
Intraoperative Findings
Two colon polyps as described (6 mm ascending colon, 4 mm sigmoid colon); otherwise normal colonic mucosa; no diverticulosis; no
masses; no active bleeding.

retrieval_messages.content:
You are an agent that gathers evidence for a claims audit by querying the
PuppyGraph knowledge graph over Cypher. You receive no pre-fetched context — you must call the
query_puppygraph tool yourself to find evidence, and may call it more than once (e.g. one query
to find a candidate, another to pull supporting detail). Only read Cypher is permitted (no
CREATE/MERGE/DELETE/SET/...).

Graph schema:

Nodes (only the attributes listed are queryable — see "Differences from plain Cypher" below).
Patient, Visit, and Claim are THREE SEPARATE NODE LABELS that all read the SAME physical `visit`
table (Patient filtered to visit_number=1, Claim filtered to claim_id IS NOT NULL) — each label
only exposes ITS OWN attribute list, not the union of all three:
  Claim         claim_review_type='APC', claim_role='claim', claim_case_id, claim_number,
                 claim_payer, claim_plan_type, claim_facility_name, claim_facility_npi,
                 claim_facility_state, claim_place_of_service, claim_attending_name,
                 claim_attending_npi, claim_attending_specialty, claim_patient_name,
                 claim_patient_mrn, claim_patient_sex, claim_patient_age, claim_dos_from,
                 claim_dos_to, claim_total_charges (claim_admit_date/claim_discharge_date/
                 claim_original_drg/claim_gap_days/etc. are DRG/Readmission/SNF-only fields,
                 always null here. NOTE: there is no `visit_id` attribute on Claim at all —
                 reach the Visit by edge traversal only)
  Line          claim_id, visit_id, line_type ('procedure' or 'diagnosis' for APC), position,
                 code_system, code, description, modifier, units, charge, revenue_code, apc —
                 APC is graded per PROCEDURE line, not per claim: each billed procedure Line
                 gets its own determination.
  Code          code_system, code, description
  MedicalRecord visit_id, claim_id, doc_kind='medical_record', review_type='APC', file_path,
                 file_name
  ClaimFile     visit_id, claim_id, doc_kind='claim_file', review_type='APC'
  Note          document_id, visit_id, claim_id, review_type='APC', note_date, text
  Policy        doc_kind='concept_workbook', review_type='APC', status='active', file_path,
                 file_name — one workbook, not payer-specific (unlike DRG/Readmission/SNF's
                 payer_guideline docs — APC's fee schedule and NCCI/technique rules apply
                 uniformly regardless of payer)
  PolicyRule    document_id, review_type='APC', rule_type ('code' / 'concept' / 'reference' /
                 'target_codes' / 'table_header' / 'concept_title' / 'empty_field'), position,
                 rule_code (e.g. 'APC-01' — every row belonging to one policy concept shares
                 this), label, text, code, status_indicator, apc, relative_weight, payment_rate

Edges:
  (Claim)-[:HAS_LINE]->(Line)-[:BILLS]->(Code)
  (PolicyRule)-[:APPLIES_TO]->(Code)             -- attrs: is_target (bool), severity
  (Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(Claim)                  -- also traversable in reverse
  (Visit)-[:DOCUMENTED_BY]->(MedicalRecord)      -- reaches the actual medical record directly
  (Visit)-[:FILED_AS]->(ClaimFile)
  (MedicalRecord)-[:HAS_NOTE]->(Note)

There are 10 APC claims, 1-3 billed procedure Lines each (verified live), matched against ~30
policy concepts (rule_code values) in one shared APC_Policy_Concepts workbook — this is a
lookup table + narrative-requirement pair, not a payer-specific guideline, so there's no
payer-matching step the way DRG/Readmission/SNF need.

Differences from plain Cypher (specific to how this graph was loaded into PuppyGraph):
- CRITICAL: a node's own id (Visit.visit_id, Claim.claim_id, PolicyRule.rule_id, etc.) is NOT
  queryable — not even to re-match that SAME node in a LATER query. Do the WHOLE hop chain you
  need in ONE query, keeping every intermediate node as a bound variable in that same query.
- Every node's OWN primary key is consumed into the vertex's internal identity and is NOT
  itself queryable. Reach nodes by EDGE TRAVERSAL, never by matching one node's FK-copy
  attribute against another node's own suppressed id.
- RETURNing a whole node (`RETURN c`) comes back as an EMPTY `{}` — always RETURN specific
  properties.
- `(Visit)-[:DOCUMENTED_BY]->(MedicalRecord)` resolves correctly here (verified live) — reaches
  the claim's actual medical record directly.
- **The APPLIES_TO edge, not TARGETS_CODE, is this graph's Code<->PolicyRule join.** Walk
  `(pr:PolicyRule {review_type:'APC', rule_type:'code'})-[rel:APPLIES_TO]->(co:Code {code:$cpt})`
  and filter `rel.is_target = true` for the row that's actually THIS concept's own billed code
  (verified live on CPT 63685: the same code also appears on unrelated `is_target:false`
  reference/comparison rows from OTHER rule_codes and a catch-all 'Master APC Reference' row —
  taking the first PolicyRule you reach without the is_target filter risks grabbing one of
  those instead of the concept that actually governs this billed code).
- The `concept`-type PolicyRule holding the actual requirement narrative is NOT reached via an
  edge from the `code`-type row — it shares the same `rule_code` property instead (verified
  live). Use get_governing_policy below rather than reconstructing this multi-rule_type join
  yourself.
- Line.modifier is graded as part of the corrected code (an exact string match including the
  modifier, e.g. "29881-59" — a right base code with the wrong/missing modifier still counts as
  wrong) — always read and state it, not just Line.code.


Domain knowledge for this review type:

APC claims audit — what this graph is for: every review is a three-way check between what was
billed (Line where line_type='procedure'), what the medical record documents (Note, reached via
the claim's own Visit -> review_type='APC' MedicalRecord), and what the governing policy
requires (the matching PolicyRule concept's `.text`, reached via get_governing_policy). A
mismatch between the claim and what the record + policy support is a Finding; if everything
lines up, it's No Finding. APC is graded per line item — each billed procedure Line gets its own
determination, not one determination for the whole claim.

Common APC Finding categories — use these as the hypotheses to check, not a checklist to
recite:
- Technique mismatch: the billed code requires a specific technique the record doesn't
  document as having actually been performed (e.g. fulguration billed, only a biopsy done).
- Extent/completeness not met: the billed code implies more was done than documented (e.g.
  tonsillectomy + adenoidectomy billed, only tonsillectomy done).
- NCCI unbundling: a component procedure billed as its own line separately from the parent
  procedure it's normally bundled into on the same session (not the same as two distinct,
  separately-dated procedures on one claim, which is legitimately two lines). Modifier 59 (or a
  more specific X{E,S,P,U} modifier) can override the edit, but only when the record
  independently documents a distinct site/session/lesion for the component code — check the
  concept's own text for exactly what has to be independently documented before accepting the
  modifier, don't accept the modifier just because it's present on the line.
- Measurement/size discrepancy: the billed code's size/diameter tier doesn't match the
  pathology report's actual measurement, or (per this dataset's concept text) the operative
  note's own intraoperative measurement — a post-fixation pathology measurement is NOT
  equivalent to the surgeon's own stated excised diameter and shouldn't be used to select the
  code tier if the two conflict.
- Site/indication mismatch: the billed code implies an anatomic site or clinical indication the
  documentation contradicts.

MANDATORY before you finalize corrected_cpt_hcpcs on any size/technique/extent-tier Finding:
verify the exact replacement code against this graph — do not answer from memory, even if
you're confident. This dataset's own code numbering does NOT necessarily match real-world CPT
numbering you may already know (verified live: a size-tier Finding answered from memory landed
on the wrong sibling code one tier off from the one this dataset's own Code table actually
assigns to that size range) — the only source of truth for "what code corresponds to this tier/
technique in THIS dataset" is this graph, never your own prior knowledge of CPT codes. Two ways
to satisfy this, depending on what the governing policy concept_text already gave you:
- If get_governing_policy's own concept_text/references already state the replacement code
  NUMBER explicitly (not just a description) — e.g. "CPT 63650 (percutaneous implantation...)
  describes..." — that IS this graph's own verified data, already retrieved; cite that number
  directly. Do not then discard it just because find_sibling_codes hasn't separately confirmed
  it, and do not give up and null the field if a find_sibling_codes guess happens to miss —
  the number you already read in the concept text is the answer.
- If the concept_text only describes a tier/criterion WITHOUT giving you an explicit code
  number (e.g. a diameter range like "2.1-3.0cm" with no code stated), call find_sibling_codes
  with keywords describing the procedure family MINUS the specific size number (e.g.
  ["malignant lesion", "trunk"], not ["2.1-3.0cm"]) to resolve that tier to an actual code —
  read the returned descriptions yourself to pick the one matching tier, and cite it.
corrected_cpt_hcpcs must never be a prose description of the tier, and never a code you haven't
seen verbatim in this graph's own data (either the concept_text you already retrieved, or
find_sibling_codes's return rows). (The one real exception: a Finding whose correction is to
remove the line entirely, e.g. an NCCI-unbundled component, or a units-only correction with no
code substitution — there, correctly, no replacement code exists to look up.)

Call get_claim_lines once (it's a bare code+description list, not something to open a policy
investigation for) so you know what else is billed on this claim. Then, if the medical record
happens to document another distinct procedure or specimen that has no match in that list, note
it — without assuming it's automatically a Finding (e.g. two same-technique procedures performed
in one session may correctly bill as a single line; a documented second lesion needing its own
code is a different story). This is a completeness check on the claim's own line list, not a
reason to go investigate every sibling line's own policy — only look further into one if the
record itself already raised a question about it.

Scoring nuance: a corrected CPT/HCPCS is graded as an exact string match INCLUDING the modifier
(Line.modifier) — the right base code with the wrong or missing modifier still counts as wrong.
Always check and state the modifier, not just the code, when you give a determination.

When searching Note for supporting text, a generic keyword (e.g. "procedure") mostly surfaces
boilerplate (consent forms, pre-op checklists) rather than the operative note detail that
actually confirms or contradicts the billed technique. Search on the specific clinical terms
instead: the anatomy/technique words from the Line.description or CPT short descriptor (e.g.
"meniscus", "resection", "debridement", the specific procedure name), and the terms named in
the policy concept's requirement text (e.g. "generator", "excised diameter", "sedation
flowsheet") — those are what the operative note is actually going to use.


Before your first tool call, briefly state your plan as a short numbered list of steps, each
corresponding to one Cypher query — keep the plan as short as the question allows, but make
sure each step is actually answerable by a single query. Revise the plan if a result surprises
you (e.g. an empty result because a field isn't queryable per the schema notes above).

You must query at least one Note passage relevant to the claim/record in question
before you are done — checking policy text alone is not enough to decide Finding vs. No
Finding, someone still has to see what the documentation actually says. Note rows
are reached by traversal (see the schema notes), and the text is long enough that you should
filter by keyword (e.g. `WHERE toLower(e.text) CONTAINS toLower('meniscus')`) rather than
pulling every passage. If you try to stop before querying any Note, you'll be
stopped and asked to check the record first.

Whenever you query Note, Fact or PolicyRule rows yourself, always RETURN the row's
id alongside its text, e.g. `RETURN id(n) AS source_id, n.title AS title, n.text AS text`. The
judgment step that reads your transcript afterward cites every passage by that source_id, and a
passage with no source_id can't be cited. The skill tools already return it.

Cypher literal strings break on an unescaped apostrophe (e.g. `CONTAINS 'patient's history'`
is a syntax error, not a match) — pick a keyword without an apostrophe, or escape it as `\'`,
rather than retrying the same broken literal.

If a more specific tool is available for a lookup (check its description), prefer it over
writing the equivalent raw Cypher yourself in query_puppygraph — it runs a traversal that's
already known to be correct, rather than one you reconstruct from the schema notes each time.

Indication for Procedure
Colorectal cancer screening, average risk, age-appropriate
The patient has failed appropriate conservative management, if applicable. The risks, benefits, and alternatives to surgery were discussed
in detail. Informed written consent was obtained as documented in the consent section. All pre-operative studies have been reviewed. The
patient was deemed an appropriate surgical candidate.
Patient Preparation & Positioning
The patient was brought to the operating room and positioned as follows: Left lateral decubitus. Standard monitoring was applied per
Continuous pulse oximetry, cardiac monitor, automated BP q5min, capnography, verbal responsiveness checks. A timeout was performed
per the Universal Protocol to confirm correct patient, correct surgical site, and correct procedure. All team members verbalized
concurrence. The operative area was prepped and draped in a sterile fashion using standard antiseptic solution.
Operative Technique - Detailed Description
After confirming patient identity, planned procedure, and consent per timeout protocol, the patient was positioned in the left lateral
decubitus position on the procedure table and standard monitors (pulse oximetry, cardiac monitor, automated blood pressure,
capnography) were applied. Moderate sedation was administered by the circulating RN per standing order beginning at 0725 (see
moderate sedation flowsheet, nursing intraop documentation, for administration and monitoring detail). Once adequate sedation depth was
confirmed, the Olympus CV-190 video colonoscope was introduced per rectum with scope insertion at 0732 (per endoscopy suite
automated procedure timer log). The scope was advanced in a retrograde fashion under direct visualization to the cecum, with the
ileocecal valve and appendiceal orifice both clearly identified, confirming a complete examination to the cecal pole. Withdrawal was then
performed with careful circumferential inspection of the mucosa.
In the ascending colon, a 6 mm sessile polyp was identified and removed in its entirety using hot snare technique in a single pass, with
immediate retrieval for pathology. In the sigmoid colon, a second, 4 mm pedunculated polyp was identified and similarly removed via hot
snare with immediate retrieval. Hemostasis was confirmed visually at both polypectomy sites without need for clip placement, injection, or
additional hemostatic intervention. No additional lesions were identified. The scope was withdrawn from the patient at 0806 (per endoscopy
suite automated procedure timer log), for a total scope insertion-to-withdrawal time of 34 minutes on that timer.
At the conclusion of the procedure, final inspection was performed to confirm hemostasis. The surgical field was irrigated. All surgical
counts were reported correct by the circulating RN and scrub tech. Dressings were applied. The patient was repositioned for transfer,
returned to baseline mental status, and transferred to the PACU in stable condition.
Intraoperative Findings
Two colon polyps as described (6 mm ascending colon, 4 mm sigmoid colon); otherwise normal colonic mucosa; no diverticulosis; no
masses; no active bleeding.

judge_messages.content:
You are a senior clinical claims auditor deciding a determination for one
billed claim line. You are given, below, everything a retrieval step already queried from a
claims/medical-record/policy knowledge graph for this line — the Cypher queries run and the
rows each one returned. You have no tool access and cannot query further; decide only from
what's shown.

Domain knowledge for this review type:

APC claims audit — what this graph is for: every review is a three-way check between what was
billed (Line where line_type='procedure'), what the medical record documents (Note, reached via
the claim's own Visit -> review_type='APC' MedicalRecord), and what the governing policy
requires (the matching PolicyRule concept's `.text`, reached via get_governing_policy). A
mismatch between the claim and what the record + policy support is a Finding; if everything
lines up, it's No Finding. APC is graded per line item — each billed procedure Line gets its own
determination, not one determination for the whole claim.

Common APC Finding categories — use these as the hypotheses to check, not a checklist to
recite:
- Technique mismatch: the billed code requires a specific technique the record doesn't
  document as having actually been performed (e.g. fulguration billed, only a biopsy done).
- Extent/completeness not met: the billed code implies more was done than documented (e.g.
  tonsillectomy + adenoidectomy billed, only tonsillectomy done).
- NCCI unbundling: a component procedure billed as its own line separately from the parent
  procedure it's normally bundled into on the same session (not the same as two distinct,
  separately-dated procedures on one claim, which is legitimately two lines). Modifier 59 (or a
  more specific X{E,S,P,U} modifier) can override the edit, but only when the record
  independently documents a distinct site/session/lesion for the component code — check the
  concept's own text for exactly what has to be independently documented before accepting the
  modifier, don't accept the modifier just because it's present on the line.
- Measurement/size discrepancy: the billed code's size/diameter tier doesn't match the
  pathology report's actual measurement, or (per this dataset's concept text) the operative
  note's own intraoperative measurement — a post-fixation pathology measurement is NOT
  equivalent to the surgeon's own stated excised diameter and shouldn't be used to select the
  code tier if the two conflict.
- Site/indication mismatch: the billed code implies an anatomic site or clinical indication the
  documentation contradicts.

MANDATORY before you finalize corrected_cpt_hcpcs on any size/technique/extent-tier Finding:
verify the exact replacement code against this graph — do not answer from memory, even if
you're confident. This dataset's own code numbering does NOT necessarily match real-world CPT
numbering you may already know (verified live: a size-tier Finding answered from memory landed
on the wrong sibling code one tier off from the one this dataset's own Code table actually
assigns to that size range) — the only source of truth for "what code corresponds to this tier/
technique in THIS dataset" is this graph, never your own prior knowledge of CPT codes. Two ways
to satisfy this, depending on what the governing policy concept_text already gave you:
- If get_governing_policy's own concept_text/references already state the replacement code
  NUMBER explicitly (not just a description) — e.g. "CPT 63650 (percutaneous implantation...)
  describes..." — that IS this graph's own verified data, already retrieved; cite that number
  directly. Do not then discard it just because find_sibling_codes hasn't separately confirmed
  it, and do not give up and null the field if a find_sibling_codes guess happens to miss —
  the number you already read in the concept text is the answer.
- If the concept_text only describes a tier/criterion WITHOUT giving you an explicit code
  number (e.g. a diameter range like "2.1-3.0cm" with no code stated), call find_sibling_codes
  with keywords describing the procedure family MINUS the specific size number (e.g.
  ["malignant lesion", "trunk"], not ["2.1-3.0cm"]) to resolve that tier to an actual code —
  read the returned descriptions yourself to pick the one matching tier, and cite it.
corrected_cpt_hcpcs must never be a prose description of the tier, and never a code you haven't
seen verbatim in this graph's own data (either the concept_text you already retrieved, or
find_sibling_codes's return rows). (The one real exception: a Finding whose correction is to
remove the line entirely, e.g. an NCCI-unbundled component, or a units-only correction with no
code substitution — there, correctly, no replacement code exists to look up.)

Call get_claim_lines once (it's a bare code+description list, not something to open a policy
investigation for) so you know what else is billed on this claim. Then, if the medical record
happens to document another distinct procedure or specimen that has no match in that list, note
it — without assuming it's automatically a Finding (e.g. two same-technique procedures performed
in one session may correctly bill as a single line; a documented second lesion needing its own
code is a different story). This is a completeness check on the claim's own line list, not a
reason to go investigate every sibling line's own policy — only look further into one if the
record itself already raised a question about it.

Scoring nuance: a corrected CPT/HCPCS is graded as an exact string match INCLUDING the modifier
(Line.modifier) — the right base code with the wrong or missing modifier still counts as wrong.
Always check and state the modifier, not just the code, when you give a determination.

When searching Note for supporting text, a generic keyword (e.g. "procedure") mostly surfaces
boilerplate (consent forms, pre-op checklists) rather than the operative note detail that
actually confirms or contradicts the billed technique. Search on the specific clinical terms
instead: the anatomy/technique words from the Line.description or CPT short descriptor (e.g.
"meniscus", "resection", "debridement", the specific procedure name), and the terms named in
the policy concept's requirement text (e.g. "generator", "excised diameter", "sedation
flowsheet") — those are what the operative note is actually going to use.


Decide per the three-way check: does the medical record, read against what the governing
policy actually requires, support the billed code? Read the documentation text carefully and
literally rather than pattern-matching on a surface word — e.g. a procedure documented as
"partial" (a partial meniscectomy, a partial tonsillectomy) is often the correct, complete,
billable term for a specific technique, not evidence that something was left incomplete; check
what the policy's own criteria actually turn on before concluding a word like "partial" means
the billed code wasn't met.

Set determination to "Insufficient Evidence" rather than guessing if what's retrieved doesn't
support a real decision either way — do not invent a Finding/No Finding to fill the gap.

system_note is the auditor note a human reviewer reads on EVERY claim, Finding or not — write
it with explicit citations (document/section/page) and reasoning a reviewer could audit line by
line; a correct determination with a
vague, citation-free note still scores as a weak note (see the quality bar in the schema
field's own description).

rationale_letter is a SEPARATE, formal appeal-ready letter to the provider — only written when
determination is Finding (null otherwise). It restates the finding and its basis for an
external, non-technical reader, not a repeat of system_note's internal auditor reasoning.

Page numbers: a medical-record note can span several PDF pages, and its page_start/page_end
are not the page of any particular line in it. In a long note's text, a [p.N] marker means the
text after it (up to the next marker) is on physical page N; cite that page in system_note,
never a note's page_start/page_end range. A note whose page_start equals its page_end is all on

Indication for Procedure
Colorectal cancer screening, average risk, age-appropriate
The patient has failed appropriate conservative management, if applicable. The risks, benefits, and alternatives to surgery were discussed
in detail. Informed written consent was obtained as documented in the consent section. All pre-operative studies have been reviewed. The
patient was deemed an appropriate surgical candidate.
Patient Preparation & Positioning
The patient was brought to the operating room and positioned as follows: Left lateral decubitus. Standard monitoring was applied per
Continuous pulse oximetry, cardiac monitor, automated BP q5min, capnography, verbal responsiveness checks. A timeout was performed
per the Universal Protocol to confirm correct patient, correct surgical site, and correct procedure. All team members verbalized
concurrence. The operative area was prepped and draped in a sterile fashion using standard antiseptic solution.
Operative Technique - Detailed Description
After confirming patient identity, planned procedure, and consent per timeout protocol, the patient was positioned in the left lateral
decubitus position on the procedure table and standard monitors (pulse oximetry, cardiac monitor, automated blood pressure,
capnography) were applied. Moderate sedation was administered by the circulating RN per standing order beginning at 0725 (see
moderate sedation flowsheet, nursing intraop documentation, for administration and monitoring detail). Once adequate sedation depth was
confirmed, the Olympus CV-190 video colonoscope was introduced per rectum with scope insertion at 0732 (per endoscopy suite
automated procedure timer log). The scope was advanced in a retrograde fashion under direct visualization to the cecum, with the
ileocecal valve and appendiceal orifice both clearly identified, confirming a complete examination to the cecal pole. Withdrawal was then
performed with careful circumferential inspection of the mucosa.
In the ascending colon, a 6 mm sessile polyp was identified and removed in its entirety using hot snare technique in a single pass, with
immediate retrieval for pathology. In the sigmoid colon, a second, 4 mm pedunculated polyp was identified and similarly removed via hot
snare with immediate retrieval. Hemostasis was confirmed visually at both polypectomy sites without need for clip placement, injection, or
additional hemostatic intervention. No additional lesions were identified. The scope was withdrawn from the patient at 0806 (per endoscopy
suite automated procedure timer log), for a total scope insertion-to-withdrawal time of 34 minutes on that timer.
At the conclusion of the procedure, final inspection was performed to confirm hemostasis. The surgical field was irrigated. All surgical
counts were reported correct by the circulating RN and scrub tech. Dressings were applied. The patient was repositioned for transfer,
returned to baseline mental status, and transferred to the PACU in stable condition.
Intraoperative Findings
Two colon polyps as described (6 mm ascending colon, 4 mm sigmoid colon); otherwise normal colonic mucosa; no diverticulosis; no
masses; no active bleeding.

result.system_note: Billed line: CPT 99153 (additional 15-minute moderate sedation unit), line 4 on claim [[CLAIM-0007]]. Governing policy (APC-03) requires the sedation intra-service interval to be measured on the sedation flowsheet (sedation start = administration of sedating agent(s); end = when recovery-readiness/hand-off criteria are met) and further states that the midpoint of the first additional 15-minute increment (approximately 23 total minutes) must be reached to support the first 99153 unit (i.e. you cannot substitute scope insertion-to-withdrawal equipment timers for the sedation flowsheet) (ev1). The medical record's sedation documentation shows sedating medications administered beginning at 07:25 (Midazolam 2 mg and Fentanyl 50 mcg, with a titration midazolam 1 mg at 07:35) (ev2), and the circulating RN documents that recovery-readiness criteria were met at 07:43 with no further sedation after 07:43 (ev3). That sequence yields an intra-service sedation interval of ~07:25-07:43 = 18 minutes by the sedation flowsheet, which is shorter than the policy's ~23 minutes required to support the first 99153 add-on unit. The operative/endoscopy equipment timer shows scope insertion at 07:32 and withdrawal at 08:06 (34 minutes), but the APC policy explicitly differentiates the sedation flowsheet from scope/equipment timers and requires reconciliation in favor of the flowsheet for 99153 (ev4, ev1). Therefore the documentation does not support this billed 99153 additional unit (line 4) - it documents less than the required midpoint/time on the sedation flowsheet. Action: remove this 99153 line (no substitute code for this line) because the record supports only the primary moderate sedation unit (99152) for the sedation interval documented. Evidence used: ev1 (policy), ev2 (med administration times), ev3 (nursing flowsheet/recovery-readiness), ev4 (operative scope timer noted but not acceptable substitute per policy).
result.rationale_letter: Re: Audit of claim [[CLAIM-0007]] (patient [[MRN-0048]]) - CPT 99153 (additional moderate sedation unit) - Finding Dear Provider, We have completed a focused audit of line 4 on claim [[CLAIM-0007]] for patient [[MRN-0048]], which billed CPT 99153 (Moderate sedation services provided by the same physician performing the diagnostic/therapeutic service; each additional 15 minutes intra-service time). The governing APC policy (APC-03) requires that intra-service moderate sedation time be measured on the sedation flowsheet (from administration of sedating agent(s) until recovery-readiness/hand-off criteria are met) and that the midpoint of the first additional 15-minute increment (approximately 23 minutes total) be reached to justify billing a 99153 add-on unit (ev1). The policy further cautions that endoscopy suite equipment timers (scope insertion-to-withdrawal) reflect instrument dwell time and are not a substitute for the sedation flowsheet (ev1). Basis for Finding: - The medication administration record documents sedating agents given at 07:25 (Midazolam 2 mg and Fentanyl 50 mcg) with a titration dose of Midazolam at 07:35 (ev2). - The circulating RN documents that recovery-readiness criteria were met at 07:43 and that no further sedation medication was given after 07:43 (ev3). Measured on the sedation flowsheet, the intra-service sedation interval is therefore approximately 07:25-07:43 = 18 minutes. - The policy requires approximately 23 minutes to reach the midpoint needed to support the first 99153 add-on unit; the documented sedation interval (18 minutes) does not meet that criterion (ev1). The scope insertion-to-withdrawal timer is 07:32-08:06 (34 minutes) (ev4), but APC policy specifies that scope/equipment timers are not equivalent to the sedation flowsheet for reporting 99153 and must not be used as a substitute (ev1). Correction Being Made: - Line 4 (CPT 99153) is not supported by the sedation flowsheet documentation and will be removed. The documentation supports the initial moderate sedation unit CPT 99152 only. If you believe additional documentation exists that documents intra-service sedation time on the administering clinician's sedation flowsheet meeting the policy's midpoint requirement (for example, a sedation flowsheet entry showing sedation start before 07:25 or recovery-readiness later than 07:48 such that >=~23 minutes of sedation is documented), please supply that specific flowsheet entry referencing the patient/chart and the time entries for reconsideration. Absent such evidence, the billed 99153 unit at line 4 is unsupported and will be disallowed. Sincerely, Clinical Claims Audit Team
